newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Turkmen leader orders 1000-day economic plan.
newsitem.headline: Turkmen leader orders 1000-day economic plan.

text.p: Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov, focus of a Stalinist personality cult, decreed on Tuesday a thousand-day economic plan aimed at dragging his energy-rich but poor desert nation into the 21st century.
In a country long on plans but short on details, Niyazov revealed little of the grandiose thousand-day scheme, saying it will be put before a People's Council at the end of the year.
But the country's former Communist Party boss kicked off the new campaign late on Monday with a lengthy harangue of his stony-faced ministers on state television.

He made clear that the republic's troubled energy sector would be milked for cash to fund the plans. This year's budget of 5,055 trillion manats, double the 1996 budget, is based on renewed exports of natural gas to western Europe.
In a first move at reforming the vital sector, Niyazov sacked oil and gas minister Gochmurad Nazdzhanov for shortcomings at the oil and gas ministry.
"All this time, all the work at the ministry has been centred on the sale of oil and gas, nobody there took care of of increasing the potential of this strategic sector," he fumed.
It is uncertain how much real weight the republic's new oil and gas minister, Batyr Sardjayev, will hold as Niyazov brooks no dissent regularly blasts and fires his ministers.

Niyazov targeted 1997 natural gas output at an ambitious 53 billion cubic metres (bcm), up from 35 bcm last year, with additional plans to produce six million tonnes of oil and gas condensate in 1997, up from last year's 4.3 million tonnes.

But the self-styled Leader of the Turkmens, whose face graces countless portraits across the capital Ashgabat and who recently had a French-made scent named after him, depends wholly on Russian pipelines for exports to paying customers.
Under a 1996 agreement with Russia's gas monopoly Gazprom GAZP.RTS, Turkmenistan is set to export about 20 bcm to western Europe this year.
Precious Turkmen hard currency revenues shrivelled in 1993 when Russia diverted its gas exports away from western Europe to cash-strapped ex-Soviet states like Ukraine.
"Debts to Turkmenistan for gas totalled $600 million in 1996 and this is dragging down our economic development," Niyazov said.
In a republic run largely as a planned economy, Niyazov also proposed to start privatising large enterprises. "With the absence of real owners, nothing will happen here," he said.
But the strategic oil and gas sector are not for sale, and there is little left in the impoverished republic to privatise.

The farm sector is still blighted by environmentally disastrous intensive cotton farming and by Niyazov's costly determination to make his country self-sufficient in grain and other agricultural produce.
"We have to spend hard currency which does not go to us on bread, milk, sugar, meat and oil," Niyazov complained. "We have every possibility of being self-sufficient."
But last year's grain harvest of 400,000 tonnes fell far short of Niyazov's 1.2 million-tonne target.
The Turkmen economy is backing away gradually from Soviet-style subsidies for food and energy.
But with wages averaging only $10-20 a month and little employment for the 3.8 million population, Turkmenistan's state-led economy appears mired in its Soviet past. $1 = 5,600 manat
